articles.title: Drop the Charges Against Misael | No Political Arrests
articles.author: Portland DSA
articles.content: Portland DSA resolutely denounces the political coercion by Texas State police of DSA member and Austin City Council candidate Misael Ramos, who was wrongfully arrested the morning of September 26. Ramos had recently attended a protest decrying ICE brutality, particularly the violence against Venezuelan immigrant Wilber Rafael Garces Perez who still remains critically injured after being shot by immigration police. Misael is one of many people in Texas being targeted for exercising their free speech in rightfully condemning state violence against the immigrant community. What we’re seeing is a racheting up of state repression, now targeting citizens and socialist political candidates. We will stand by our people, immigrants and poor alike, against this violence. Portland DSA demands the charges be dropped against Misael and that Wilber be released to his family. We also echo calls by DSA to the following : Now is the time for an escalation of demands, not cowardice or inaction. We can and must fight back, at every level of power we hold. Therefore, we further demand: Austin City Council and ALL Texas cities and counties must push back against unconstitutional state laws, reintroduce Sanctuary City policies, and CEASE and REFUSE any and all collaboration on immigration enforcement; The Texas state legislature must REPEAL state laws that prevent cities from governing themselves (like SB 4 (2017), SB 4 (2023), SB 8, HB 1900, and HB 2127) and return local control to local governments; The governor must END Operation Lone Star and use the billions of wasted taxpayer dollars to fund communities instead; Texas cities and counties must BAN all AI surveillance tech like automated license plate readers (ALPRs) across the state that are used DAILY to track and arrest our community members, provided through contracts with Flock, Axon, and other companies; The federal government must HALT all deportations now and reunite all the families who have been forcibly separated; We must ABOLISH the current violent immigration enforcement system and instead establish a new system that includes a meaningful pathway to citizenship for all those who call the United States home. Abolish ICE. Abolish CBP. Abolish DHS. No one is free until everyone is free. In solidarity, Portland DSA

articles.title: American Capitalism Isn’t Just Billionaires
articles.author: Daniel Colligan
articles.content: When one thinks of the rich in the United States, the first people who come to mind are the megabillionaires whose extravagant consumption, eye-popping wealth, and notorious political interventions have transformed them into household names. Perched atop the Forbes 400 list of America’s richest individuals are Silicon Valley moguls and Wall Street executives who command some of the most prominent corporations in America. Beneath this elite stratum of capitalists lies a vastly less conspicuous group of still-wealthy but lesser-known business owners. Far more numerous and more geographically dispersed across the country than their billionaire brethren, this “ American Gentry ” exercises great influence on local, state, and even national politics. The relatively scant attention they receive compared to their headline-grabbing compatriots means that their collective effect on the American wealth distribution has been hitherto mostly unexamined. A new book by Princeton economist Owen Zidar and University of Chicago economist Eric Zwick attempts to correct this relative neglect by quantifying the place of “ The Everywhere Millionaire ” in the American wealth distribution. The book is a popular exposition of previous academic work that celebrated scholars of inequality Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman deemed (despite some critiques) an “important contribution” to the estimation of wealth inequality in the United States. What emerges from Zidar and Zwick’s investigations is the fundamental role of “pass-through” businesses in securing their owners a place near the top of the American wealth distribution. Changes to the tax code in the past half century, some lobbied for by the very business owners receiving their benefits, have made the pass-through business structure even more profitable than it would have been otherwise. The result is an astounding amount of wealth collected by the American Gentry, who often employ it toward corrosive, self-serving political ends. Do Not Pass Through, Do Not Collect $200 Zidar and Zwick coin the term “Main Street Millionaires” (MSMs) to signify households with at least $5 million in wealth (meaning they are in the top 4 percent of the US wealth distribution) and private business ownership. This group, around three million in number, collectively owns an impressive thirteen times the combined wealth of the Forbes 400. The collective wealth of the MSMs has more than doubled over the course of the twenty-first century, to the point where it presently stands at around $55 trillion. MSMs are also more geographically dispersed than their Forbes 400 colleagues. Half of the latter live in New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles, or Miami, whereas less than a quarter of the MSMs do. The businesses that MSMs run are often classified as pass-through entities in the tax code, which include sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability companies, and S corporations. Unlike a C corporation, which treats the company as a separate taxpaying entity from its owners, pass-throughs do not pay corporate or dividend taxes, and instead their profits pass through to the owners’ individual income taxes. The Tax Reform Act of 1986, which pushed the top individual tax rate below the corporate tax rate for several years, triggered a major shift in the legal structure of American business. The result is that today 95 percent of all US businesses are pass-throughs, accounting for the employment of half of all American workers and more than half of American business income. Indeed, Zidar and Zwick and other coauthors have calculated that 41 percent of the rise in the income share of the top 1 percent of Americans since 1980 is due to pass-through income. With almost all US businesses now classified as pass-throughs of one sort or another, the businesses the MSMs own run the gamut of American commerce. Zidar and Zwick profile businesses that manufacture everything from seamless gutters to tanning beds to laboratory chemicals to quiche and provide services that span from ambulance billing to trade show planning. It should be stressed, however, that private business is not necessarily small business. Major corporations such as Fidelity and Hobby Lobby are registered as pass-throughs, while large firms like Koch and Mars are private C corporations. But even more modest MSMs can generate serious profits, as the authors demonstrate with some revealing figures. For instance, “there are 25 autodealers [in the top 0.1 percent of the US income distribution] for every member of the Forbes 400.” Previous attempts to more comprehensively map the upper reaches of the wealth distribution used one of three methodologies, all of which generated results but had various shortcomings: surveys, investigative reporting, and nonlinked databases. Surveys have limited coverage, face difficulty cajoling the rich to disclose information about their financial situation, and are sometimes subject to anonymization procedures precisely to prevent users from linking the data to identifiable persons. Investigative reporting’s reach is inherently limited; even the people behind cataloging the Forbes 400 can’t be certain that they are not overlooking less ostentatious billionaires. Finally, nonlinked databases are not as useful as those that can match their data to others. Zidar and Zwick instead follow the lead of Thomas Piketty and his collaborators in using tax data as their fundamental data source. The core methodological innovation informing the book’s findings is the linkage of tax databases within the US Department of the Treasury to match businesses to their owners and employees (all anonymized). The authors then combed through auxiliary sources, such as registries of private jet and yacht owners, to attempt to deanonymize these millionaires. Resulting interviews with various capitalists the authors identified comprise a significant portion of the book. Zidar and Zwick frame their findings as a contrarian exercise highlighting how much relatively unassuming professions contribute to the upper layers of the American wealth distribution. However, some of the evidence they present in the book qualifies this narrative. A table showing the industries generating the most pass-through income is heavily populated by the highly paid professions one might expect: lawyers, doctors, financiers, accountants, dentists, realtors, architects, and consultants. To be sure, plenty of more plebeian businesses are represented as well: lumberyards, motorcycle dealers, and paper product distributors, for instance, and these less glamorous trades are often the focus of the book’s anecdotes. The Everywhere Bilker Part of the story of the MSMs’ affluence is the squeezing of their workers. Smaller businesses are legally exempt from many of the labor protections that larger corporations must enforce. For instance, the Family and Medical Leave Act only applies to firms with fifty or more employees, portions of the Civil Rights Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act only fully apply at a fifteen-employee threshold, the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act only regulates employers with at least one hundred workers, and the Affordable Care Act’s requirement that businesses provide their employees health insurance only kicks in at a minimum of fifty employees. On top of these difficulties, smaller shops are notoriously harder to unionize. Zidar and Zwick briefly weigh in on the controversy regarding why labor faces an ongoing decline in its share of national income. One factor they highlight as driving this trend is the increasing use of noncompete agreements to discourage workers — now even low-paid and entry-level ones — from switching employers. In previous work, Zidar and Zwick and coauthors suggested that a third of the declining labor share was a statistical artifact created by the classification of many American businesses as pass-through entities. When assessing the effect of MSMs on politics, it’s noteworthy that MSMs themselves make up a significant share of American politicians. Nearly a quarter of congressional representatives own a business, as do over 40 percent of legislators at the state level and a third of all mayoral candidates. This means that a large share of legislators have a personal incentive to support the interests of business owners generally and individually will be tempted to promote their own business interests. MSMs have secured anticompetitive legal protection of their businesses in a variety of industries, pushing up costs for consumers. Beer distributors, for example, benefit from laws that prevent brewers from also owning distribution and make it difficult to terminate a distribution contract. Franchise laws give auto dealers similar protection from rivals. Realtors guarantee their positions as middlemen by restricting access to information about real estate sales. Doctors inflate their profits through restricting access to medical care, which they do by putting a ceiling on the number of residency positions and limiting the ability of nonphysicians to deliver care. Powerful sectional lobbies ensure the maintenance of their members’ privileges through organizations like the National Association of Realtors, American Medical Association, and National Automobile Dealers Association. MSMs skew politically conservative, and some of them have unsurprisingly used their fortunes to advance right-wing causes. In 2022, the largest federal campaign donors for Republicans were Dick and Liz Uihlein, whose income derives from the shipping supplies company Uline. The late Republican senator and presidential nominee John McCain ’s political career was largely funded by his wife’s inherited riches from a beer distribution company. The MSMs’ political influence has been most nefarious, perhaps, in the domain of taxes. The Internal Revenue Service estimates that around $600 billion dollars of taxes are owed but not paid every year; pass-through owners are responsible for almost half of this “ tax gap .” “More than at any recent time,” Zidar and Zwick write, “the tax code for pass-throughs runs on the honor system, with predictable results.” And MSMs are progressively seeing more tax loopholes enacted to their benefit. Estate taxes have been whittled down to the point where only 0.1 percent of households face an estate tax of any sort. The 2017 Trump tax cuts allowed pass-through owners to deduct 20 percent of business income from their taxes, and the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act made these temporary provisions permanent. Dream On Even though Zidar and Zwick recognize that upward social mobility is becoming more difficult in the United States, a major theme of the book is that the “ American Dream ” of upward mobility remains attainable, primarily through private business ownership. The authors plainly have admiration for the MSMs who have achieved entrepreneurial success, and much of the text is content drawn from interviews with MSMs about their achievements. Clearly the authors intended these profiles both as ways to de-anonymize the “stealthy wealthy” and to give their account some narrative color, but the stream of self-reported business heroics of various MSMs becomes tedious. Despite large chunks of the book reading as inspirational literature for aspiring business owners (the largest of three segments is entitled “How To Get Rich”) or a celebration of the everyman capitalist, Zidar and Zwick recognize the negative effects of MSMs in exacerbating social inequality. They end the book with some policy reform proposals, such as raising the minimum wage and reforming the tax code to harmonize tax rates. Useful steps, of course, but these proposals fall far short of a comprehensive program to rein in the economic and political power of the MSMs. The main value in Zidar and Zwick’s book, however, is not in its politics but in its empirical research. The authors have gone some distance toward unmasking a stratum of the capitalist class that too often escapes recognition, not to mention criticism. A serious left-wing political project needs to grapple with this overlooked but powerful section of the American elite. articles.title: Big Idea: Vinyl
articles.content: 1 . an analog sound format requiring physical care and attention 2 . a small act of rebellion against the algorithm Kurt Vonnegut (a former In These Times senior editor, by the way!) once told a story about refusing to buy 100 envelopes online: ​ “ I’m going to have a hell of a good time in the process of buying one envelope,” he said. ​ “ I meet a lot of people.” The moral, he said, was that we’re here to enjoy the world and the people in it, a facet of human life computers have changed. Vinyl is the envelope. It makes you leave the house. ​ “ And, of course, the computers will do us out of that,” he said. But ​ “ what the computer people don’t realize, or they don’t care, is we’re dancing animals. We love to move around. And we’re not supposed to dance at all anymore.” We have better technology, so why regress? For one, ​ “ better” is doing a lot of work. Spotify’s default streaming quality is compressed (some of the original audio data is stripped out to save space), which is why more than a few hard-core music lovers call it mid. (Vinyl has its own trade-offs, but at least nothing’s being thrown away to save space.) Vinyl also forces you to listen to an album in the artist’s intended order, rather than a shuffle algorithm’s best guess at what keeps you listening longest. Plus, who doesn’t love nostalgia? A friend with a sizable inherited record collection put it this way: ​ “ I don’t listen to rock daily, but when I put on Cheap Trick, I’m like, damn, that’s my dad’s favorite album.” Why spend money on records? Because that $ 12 . 99 streaming subscription money doesn’t go to artists. Spotify’s Daniel Ek is worth nearly $ 13 billion, and co-founder Martin Lorentzon nearly $ 12 billion. Meanwhile, artists earn, on average, $ 0 . 003 to $ 0 . 005 per stream. Björk called Spotify ​ “ the worst thing that could happen to musicians,” pushing artists to tour constantly just to stay solvent. In 2025 , Massive Attack pulled its catalog entirely, calling Spotify an ​ “ economic burden” funneling fans’ money into ​ “ lethal, dystopian technologies.” Buying a record (or a CD!) sends money directly to an artist or a small shop, instead of to a platform where songs have to be streamed hundreds of times to earn the artist a single dollar. It’s not really more expensive— it’s expensive differently and more honestly. What if we all become hipsters? I get the concern. But buying used vinyl and CDs is reuse, not consumerism dressed up in flannel. A physical collection is a hobby with something to show for it — different from a rented catalog you lose the day you stop paying.

articles.title: Eric Hobsbawm Owed His Success to Mass Culture
articles.author: Erik Linstrum
articles.content: More than the “revolutionary historian” promised by the subtitle, the Eric Hobsbawm chronicled in Emile Chabal’s biography is above all a canny academic entrepreneur. Early in his career, Hobsbawm found a literary agent and converted his lectures for undergraduates into a series of best-selling books. He made valuable contacts with rising-star scholars and publishing houses in continental Europe. He traveled widely: not so much for archival research, which he practiced sparingly, but for conferences, lectures, and intellectual tourism in appealing destinations. The Soviet Union, which occupied a central place in his thought for obvious reasons, did not qualify for more than a brief, unpleasant visit. He displayed a knack for keeping himself in the public eye, with a steady stream of journalism and polemics, and for a degree of tactical adaptation. In the 1980s, he pivoted from writing the histories of the working class that defined his early work to studies of nationalism and invented traditions. By the late 1990s, he had achieved such eminence that he could turn down a knighthood while requesting — and receiving — a considerably more prestigious and exclusive appointment to the Order of the Companions of Honour, an award also tied to the monarchy but with less symbolic baggage. Eric Hobsbawm, Careerist? If all this sounds less than flattering, it isn’t because Chabal has written a hatchet job. On the contrary: The Age of Hobsbawm is admiring of the historian’s accomplishments while mercifully free of the emotional overinvestments he inspired in earlier generations. The absence of tedious Cold War moralism — alternately prosecutorial or tortured on such questions as Hobsbawm’s failure to leave the party after 1956 or his enjoyment of establishment privileges — is refreshing. Chabal offers a decidedly twenty-first century perspective, concerned more with explaining the global phenomenon that was Hobsbawm than judging the man or seeking to revive his ideas. But the line between demythologization and deflation is thin. Turning a high-resolution lens on the sausage-making of academic advancement and intellectual reputation-building is bound to leave any subject diminished. While some of the details will be familiar to those who have read Richard Evans’s 2019 biography, Chabal’s cool-eyed appraisal repeatedly brings the legend down to earth. As a supervisor of graduate students, Hobsbawm was usually inattentive, veering into downright hostility to approaches he disliked: women’s and feminist histories foremost among them. He never made peace with the New Left sensibility that took gender and race as seriously as class. For all his interest in cultural production — an enthusiasm shaped, though not straitjacketed, by the Marxist catechism of base and superstructure — his tastes were fusty. He found jazz a worthwhile topic in the 1950s only insofar as it met his standards for popular authenticity, which meant embodying black folk traditions while retaining mass commercial appeal. For a man whose aesthetics were enduringly forged in the same 1930s youth as his politics, Miles Davis and John Coltrane missed the mark. As for the actually existing popular music of rock and roll, Hobsbawm thought Elvis Presley “peculiarly unappealing” and wrote dismissively of the Beatles that “anyone can produce that sound.” Old-fashioned in some ways, Hobsbawm was extremely well matched to his time in others. The success of his books reflected their timeliness. The massive expansion of higher education on both sides of the Atlantic created demand for accessible introductions to economic history, such as his Industry and Empire (1968), and modern Europe, covered in the famous tetralogy that began with The Age of Revolution (1962). The “paperback revolution” described by historian Peter Mandler solidified the market for serious nonfiction in affordable editions. Not least, Marxism enjoyed enormous intellectual cachet — and a mass following — in societies as disparate as Italy, India, and Brazil. The Eurocentrism of the Ages volumes, so conspicuous in retrospect, mattered less at a time when many of the most pressing Marxist debates — about the demise of feudalism, the advent of industrial production, and the immiseration of workers — were being waged on the terrain of British history. Little wonder that Hobsbawm’s work repeatedly circled back to what he saw as the formation of mass society in the late nineteenth century. Universal education, rising literacy, new communication technologies, a popular press: these were not just the preconditions for nationalism, democracy, and ideological politics in the fin de siècle. They were also the foundations, in a more distant way, of Hobsbawm’s success in the literary marketplace. The volume devoted to the late nineteenth century, The Age of Empire (1987), marked a turning point in the series, arguing that the forces that destabilized and ultimately destroyed bourgeois society emerged from the triumphant capitalist order it had built. Hobsbawm doubtless savored the irony, in his own career, of leveraging the commercial incentives of the book business to deliver left-wing history to hundreds of thousands of readers. An Annaliste From the Anglosphere Particularly in the Ages series, it is difficult to disentangle Marxism from other historiographical influences. It is also true that the tetralogy is at its least convincing when it hews most closely to orthodox Marxism. Yes, the elegant architecture of the series derives from the interlocking advance of a new mode of production (industrial capitalism), a new social grouping (the bourgeoisie), and a new ideology (liberalism). But this master narrative strains to meet the facts at crucial moments. Hobsbawm’s interpretation of the French Revolution — one half of the “dual revolution” that kicks off the series — in the strict class terms of a “bourgeois revolution” was outdated almost as soon as the ink was dry. The risk of historiographical obsolescence became more acute as the interval between volumes lengthened; by the 1980s, historians were questioning whether the bourgeoisie anywhere in nineteenth-century Europe was really so triumphant in the face of what Arno Mayer called “the persistence of the old regime.” At the same time, as Chabal points out, Hobsbawm’s decision to elevate political principles of liberty and equality to the same explanatory rank as the Industrial Revolution marked a bold departure from strictly materialist analysis. It is something of a cliché to describe Hobsbawm as cosmopolitan because of his birth in Alexandria, childhood in Vienna, and adolescence in Berlin. The label fits best as a statement of his role as an intellectual intermediary, bringing elements of the French Annales school into mainstream Anglophone historiography at a time when few others were doing so. I am less sure than Chabal that “total history” is the right term for the Ages series; Fernand Braudel’s The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (1949) and Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie’s Montaillou (1975) traded specific geographic boundaries for depths of environmental and anthropological texture not captured by the ostensibly global scale on which Hobsbawm was working. Marxist annalistes such as Ernest Labrousse, who in 1955 issued a prominent call for a history of the nineteenth-century bourgeoisie, represent a more obvious influence. But if Hobsbawm and the other towering figure of his generation of British historians, E. P. Thompson, both subordinated high politics to social history, Hobsbawm’s route to that destination — reflected in the pages of tables and charts that adorned many of his books — was paved with the quantitative data that the Annales valued so highly. Without ever bogging down the fluent prose of the Ages series, price cycles and export volumes provided the materialist grounding for Hobsbawm’s confident pronouncements on everything from urban planning and domestic architecture to music, painting, and literature. Looking Back That confidence in the power of empirically derived data, Chabal shows, might be the most British thing about Hobsbawm. He was a product of the Oxbridge system in his talent for generalizing from well-chosen details, though probably no one could do it as artfully. A flair for what Hobsbawm himself called haute vulgarisation served him well as a university lecturer and is the reason that the Ages books remain so readable today. Unlike Thompson, Hobsbawm did not forsake high culture along with high politics, and his sympathetic interest in popular protest did not foreclose writing about the likes of Ludwig van Beethoven, Honoré de Balzac, and Albert Einstein. Hobsbawm’s identification with “history from below,” more pronounced in some works than others, was always more equivocal than for some of his peers — perhaps because, at least to some degree, he absorbed and accepted the cultural values of the Bildungsbürgertum . Chabal emphasizes the critical edge of Hobsbawm’s take on the superficiality and artificiality of the bourgeois world. But there was also nostalgia, or at least ambivalence, in Hobsbawm’s attitude to the class that dominated his magnum opus. In the introduction to The Age of Empire , the historian’s affective connection to the era in which his parents came of age inspired some of his most lyrical lines: For all of us there is a twilight zone between history and memory. . . . For individual human beings this zone stretches from the point where living family traditions or memories begin . . . to the end of infancy, when public and private destinies are recognized as inseparable. . . . It is itself an incoherent, incompletely perceived image of the past, sometimes more shadowy, sometimes apparently precise, always transmitted by a mixture of learning and second-hand memory shaped by public and private tradition. For it is still part of us, but no longer quite within our personal reach. The tantalizing proximity, yet ultimate inaccessibility, of those years before 1914 is especially poignant because Hobsbawm’s parents died young. But there is a hint of social as well as personal loss, a longing for the solidity of the bourgeois order swept away by the war. The final volume in the series, The Age of Extremes (1994), has an unmoored quality as violent events overwhelm structures and processes in the maelstrom of what Hobsbawm termed “the short twentieth century.” The better companion for the first three Ages volumes is arguably Peter Gay’s The Bourgeois Experience (1984–1998), the work of another Jewish émigré from Central Europe, born six years after Hobsbawm, though with Sigmund Freud rather than Karl Marx as the theoretical lodestar. In different ways, both works are about the “fragility” and the “tenuous grip” of bourgeois dominance (to borrow from Chabal’s gloss on Hobsbawm). The twentieth century might have appeared less disjunctive in Hobsbawm’s telling if colonial violence had featured more prominently all along. The treatment of the Haitian Revolution as an afterthought in The Age of Revolution is symptomatic of the series as a whole: the world-systems weighting of “center” and “periphery” applies not only to capitalist development but to ideas, experiences, and people as well. Even The Age of Empire fails to live up to its title in large part because Hobsbawm leans so heavily on the Hobsonian-Leninist model of imperialism as an outgrowth of monopoly capitalism. It is a book about the “apotheosis” and “destruction” of the bourgeoisie, Chabal writes, while the human catastrophe of imperial conquest is reduced to the abstract “terms of a political and historiographical debate that needed to be settled.” Even on Hobsbawm’s own terms, this focus on Europe represents a missed opportunity, because the vulnerability of the bourgeoisie was nowhere more acute than in the colonial outposts that strove to replicate European society far from home. Though he famously refused to join Thompson and others in leaving the Communist Party of Great Britain in 1956, Hobsbawm emerged from the shattering of its intellectual milieu with a more flexible and questioning attitude to the party line, producing some of his most interesting work as a consequence. His 1959 book Primitive Rebels took seriously the political aspirations of peasant uprisings far removed from the industrial proletariat privileged by Marxist theory. His later work on nationalism discussed ideological regimes of collective identity with only limited reference to material causes. Where Hobsbawm evolved least was almost certainly in his Eurocentrism: an imperfect term, not least because it masks the novelty of his attention to the ways that global and imperial forces remade Europe. It would be difficult to imagine Sven Beckert’s “war capitalism” or Kenneth Pomeranz’s “ghost acres,” for instance, without the pioneering argument of Industry and Empire , which linked the onset of the Industrial Revolution to the demand boost of imperial expansion. Of course, Hobsbawm’s books will continue to be read for the sheer artistry of their craft: the subordination of narrative to structure, the fluency in shifting between macro and micro scales, the promiscuous variety of sources, the plain yet vigorous expository prose. Yet his reluctance to wrestle with topics that most historians today would consider central — genocide and decolonization — shows that the path for history after Hobsbawm is not only a matter of geographical rebalancing. Rather than writing Europe out of the story, we must write about it differently: no longer as the cradle of an immanent logic of history but as the cockpit of a violent, acquisitive, sometimes irrational, and often unpredictable project of domination whose consequences we have yet to fully grasp. articles.title: The Bosses’ Oldest Dream
articles.author: Garrison Lovely
articles.content: The English inventor Charles Babbage is best remembered for his work designing the foundations for all digital computers with Ada Lovelace in the nineteenth century. What’s lesser known is why he wanted to build them. In the decades leading up to the British Empire’s abolition of slavery in the West Indies in 1833 (which Babbage supported), there was a serious question of how to get free and rebellious industrial workers to produce enough to sustain the empire. Babbage’s answer was to surveil workers and divide their efforts into standardized, measurable tasks — a project he saw as a necessary step on the way to automating labor entirely. Babbage didn’t invent these methods, as Meredith Whittaker, an artificial intelligence scholar who coled Google’s 2018 walkout, writes in a Logic(s) essay . Similar technologies of labor control were developed first on plantations to extract maximum labor from enslaved people, with management guides routinely circulating among British capitalists. “Babbage’s proto-Taylorist ideas on how to discipline workers are inextricably connected to the calculating engines he spent his life attempting to build,” Whittaker writes. Automation gave bosses a tool to replace striking workers and provided a disciplinary check, in Babbage’s words, “against the inattention, the idleness, or the dishonesty of human agents.” There’s a neat alpha and omega quality to computing: its ultimate effort, the Obsoleting Project — the industry’s drive to build machines that can do all our jobs — rhymes with its earliest. Should they work as intended, those machines would act as the tireless, pliant, cheap workers that bosses could previously only dream of. From Babbage to Bezos, managers have always resented the various ways that humans aren’t optimized for output — and therefore, their bottom line. For bosses, cost savings alone are only part of the attraction. Automation also weakens workers’ bargaining power and is used to make organizing even harder. After workers alleged Amazon used algorithmic management to surveil and stifle protected labor organizing, Stanford Law Lecturer Seema N. Patel told The Guardian that AI lets employers discipline hundreds of thousands of workers “in a way that no human manager or group of managers could even do.” “You feel like you’re in prison,” Wendy Taylor, an Amazon packer, said . “They know every move you make, when you’re working, when you’re not working.” Of course, Amazon is also leading the charge on replacing workers entirely. Yoshua Bengio is the most-cited living scientist thanks to his foundational contributions to deep learning. “I’m talking to a lot of CEOs around the world,” he told me, “and they’ll automate [jobs] as fast as they possibly can.” Indeed, a 2025 World Economic Forum survey of more than one thousand large employers found more than 40 percent planned to reduce their workforce as a result of automation by 2030. Companies are also creating more wealth with fewer people than ever. Per employee, the world’s most valuable companies in recent decades were worth anywhere from $3.5 million to as much as $30 million. Nvidia? More than $100 million. Pure AI firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI have pushed the trend even further, with ratios between $140 million and $167 million. This surge in AI-driven wealth concentration builds on a decades-long rise in inequality. As the economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman have shown , inequality levels in the United States are the highest they’ve been since the 1920s. If machines can truly substitute for human labor across the board, the result could look like a worldwide game of musical chairs, where your economic position is determined by whatever wealth you happened to have at the moment your work stopped being worth paying for. Looking at this data, AI appears less a bolt from the blue than the next — and perhaps final — frontier in the endless pursuit of profit. Can They Really Do It? It probably comes as little surprise to you that many capitalists want to automate their workers away. But can they? The question is difficult to answer definitively. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei sounded the alarm in mid-2025, predicting what Axios dubbed a “white-collar bloodbath.” AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and spike overall unemployment to 10 to 20 percent in the next one to five years, he told the publication. Of course, to skeptics, the CEO of an AI company warning that its technology would be so effective it would soon replace human workers was nothing more than a savvy earned media campaign. But that’s hard to square with more recent reporting that OpenAI blocked its economists from publishing research that showed its technology was displacing jobs. By 2025, signs of AI’s deleterious effects on the workforce appeared to be everywhere. Rising unemployment for college graduates, dips in job postings, and dramatic Big Tech layoffs were all pointing the same way, and software engineer hiring in particular cratered. People were quick to attribute the drop to AI. However, as keen observers noted, the plunge in hiring coincided more neatly with the Fed’s increases to interest rates than with the rise of ChatGPT, which didn’t become much of a coder until after net hiring had (barely) resumed. Generative AI rose to prominence at around the same time as today’s turbulent macroeconomic and political conditions, making it fiendishly difficult to explain changes. Anecdata in the form of news stories about young people struggling to find programming jobs won’t cut it. I hate to say it, but this sounds like a job for economists. In 2024, when Daron Acemoglu — who would go on to share that year’s Nobel Prize in economics — predicted the labor market effects of AI over the next decade, people took notice. Against Goldman Sachs and McKinsey predictions that AI would add trillions to GDP, he expected a nothingburger, forecasting that US GDP would only be around 1 percent higher in ten years due to AI. Economists mostly don’t believe there’s any real chance AI could put most people out of work anytime soon, Stanford economics postdoc Phil Trammell told me, but Acemoglu’s view is even “more pessimistic than the mainstream.” On the opposite end of the spectrum is Anton Korinek, a University of Virginia economist on leave at Anthropic since March, who uses standard economic models to look at what might happen if firms can effectively turn capital into more labor. Assuming full automation is reached in twenty years (“baseline AGI”), he and his PhD student Donghyun Suh predict the economy would double over the subsequent decade. If it’s possible in five years (“aggressive AGI”), they predict a tripling of GDP by 2034 — ten times faster growth than the business-as-usual scenario. “However,” they write, “wages collapse as the economy approaches full automation.” “Economists have been telling the rest of the world for the past 200 years that we shouldn’t worry about automation,” Korinek told me, “because if you destroy some jobs, the economy always creates new ones.” That was true in the past, he acknowledged, but only because “there were always things that only humans could do.” Indeed, there are more people than ever before, with more jobs than ever before, even after more than two centuries of automation. However, we’ve never had a machine that can actually make labor. (Korinek has separately clarified he’s not predicting imminent AGI himself, but rather using traditional economics to show what would happen if the predictions of AI experts like Geoffrey Hinton actually came to pass.) Economic forecasts are notoriously sensitive to their underlying assumptions. Acemoglu’s 2024 paper uses mainstream ways to measure a task’s automation potential. But when it comes to AI’s capabilities, he takes a distinctly conservative approach, assuming they won’t significantly advance beyond GPT-4’s, which was the state of the art at the time. Trammell told me that the difference between the Acemoglu and Korinek camps comes down to “whether the economic impacts of AI over the next ten years will be mainly about the diffusion of what AI could already do as of a year ago versus the things it becomes able to do over the next ten years.” That’s not really an economics question, Trammell said. “It’s a question about technological forecasting. I think reasonable people can disagree about it. But it’s also not Daron’s wheelhouse.” In September 2025, I interviewed Acemoglu for a Nobel Foundation panel during the United Nations General Assembly. To my surprise, he said he was going to “stick to his guns.” In a late 2024 interview , he had argued that the productivity story depends on the technology creating genuinely new tasks and new products, and he doesn’t see the industry’s current focus delivering much of that within a decade. He expects near-term gains to concentrate in relatively “easy-to-learn” white-collar tasks, while jobs that rely on tacit judgment, social interaction, and hard-to-verify outcomes remain far less exposed. It is true that, even years after the release of ChatGPT, it’s been hard to find evidence that AI is actually killing jobs. An October 2025 Yale study using the standard dataset for labor economists, the US Current Population Survey (CPS), found that “currently, measures of exposure, automation, and augmentation show no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment.” Also in October, when I asked Korinek about the data to date, he admitted that we only have “tiny little bits of empirical evidence that are not rising to the level of transformativeness.” So, “if you say I’m an honest evidence-bound economist, it’s still fair to say that the evidence doesn’t suggest that this is different from any prior technological revolution.” But focusing on whole occupations may miss the early signs of automation. This is where three Stanford economists stepped in with a groundbreaking paper in August 2025 . Rather than rely on traditional government sources like CPS, which offer a useful — but bird’s-eye — view of employment changes, they got their hands on data from a payroll processor, allowing them to zoom in on trends too subtle to spot otherwise. Spoiler: the anecdotes were a real sign that the white-collar bloodbath was already well underway, and like the 1918 flu, it claimed young people most. With payroll data going back to 2021, the authors split professions into six age cohorts, starting with twenty-two- to twenty-five-year-olds, and bucketed jobs by AI exposure using the same metric as Acemoglu. The most exposed were in fields like programming and customer service. After controlling for interest rates, pandemic-era overhiring, and other factors, the data tells no clear story at first. Even for the youngest, most AI-exposed workers, relative employment bounced around for years, declining as much as 6 percent in 2022 before recovering to zero in mid-2024. But then it falls off a cliff, plummeting 16 percent in just over a year, with little sign of stopping. By late 2025, the macro data looked consistent with this story. The US economy grew at 4.3 percent in the third quarter — the fastest in two years — while job creation averaged an anemic 51,000 per month. Joseph Brusuelas, the chief economist at the accounting firm RSM, writes , “The great decoupling of jobs and growth will take some explaining to the American public.” The Stanford paper offers one compelling explanation. Who Else Stands to Lose? Korinek worries that we’re heading toward something more fundamental than a rough patch for entry-level coders. “The main economic risk under AI,” he told me, “is that it will fundamentally undermine labor, that it will lead to essentially a large part of the population becoming losers of this technology.” He observed that wage labor was “basically a construct of the industrial age” — one not likely to survive long term under AGI, where, by default, he expected labor to “experience a very significant devaluation.” The rise of automation in the United States is happening after decades of declining union density, with just 6 percent of private sector workers belonging to one. Currently, labor automation mostly doesn’t look like mass layoffs; instead the Stanford paper suggests firms will increasingly avoid hiring anyone they might be able to automate — a group that will grow larger as AI improves. And since AI labor is typically orders of magnitude cheaper than the human variety, substitution doesn’t require that AI be as good, just good enough . Collective Power After years reporting on the Obsoleting Project, I’ve found that lawmakers won’t stop it unless we make them. The industry has captured them, and they were already catastrophically insulated from what the public wants. What has slowed automation down, where anything has, is workers organizing. One place where bosses tried — but largely failed — to use automation to reduce labor power was in scriptwriting. To better understand how, I spoke to Ellen Stutzman, the chief negotiator for the Writers Guild of America (WGA) 2023 strike. She told me that AI concerns emerged organically from what members were already experiencing: a speedup. As streaming replaced broadcast television over the preceding fifteen years, studios shifted from fewer shows with twenty-two-episode seasons to more shows with just eight-episode seasons, asking writers to do more work in less time for less money. The writers were already going into the strike seeking contractual minimums on staffing levels and time to do jobs. So when ChatGPT arrived, it looked like the natural progression of that trend. “It’s like one writer with an AI system doing an entire season,” Stutzman said, “or eventually no writers.” The WGA didn’t go into bargaining demanding a ban on AI. Instead, it wanted restrictions on how the technology was used, namely for AI-generated material to be treated the way Wikipedia articles were — as research, not writing. If a studio hands a writer AI-generated material, the writer should still get full credit and compensation. Whatever the machine spits out doesn’t count as literary material under the contract. And writers shouldn’t be forced to use AI tools. That last one mattered, she said, because members’ views ran the whole spectrum: “People like David Simon, who was on the negotiating committee, who I think said, ‘I would rather put a gun in my mouth than use AI.’” It was only on the final weekend before the contract deadline, Stutzman said, that the studios were willing to say anything at all about AI. At that point, they finally pointed to language in the existing collective bargaining agreement saying that a “writer” is a human being and told the guild that, at least on paper, AI could not be credited as the writer. But they stressed that they did not want to limit how they might use the technology in practice. This coincided with concerns over studios using AI to scan actors to create “synthetic performers” for background shots. The Screen Actors Guild–American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) launched its own strike a few months later, in which the use of digital replicas became a key sticking point. It took a five-month strike to get the protections writers wanted, and Stutzman is clear-eyed about the limits of what they achieved: the WGA has no power over any AI company. “What we can do in a collective bargaining agreement is regulate our employers,” she said, “but OpenAI is not our employer.” The companies that scraped writers’ work to train their models remain beyond the guild’s direct reach — a problem the WGA is now trying to address through litigation and legislation. Against this bleak backdrop, I asked Stutzman what other automation-exposed workers could learn from their experience. She didn’t hesitate. “It’s the same lesson I have on everything, which is about collective power,” she said. “If you want to push back, if you want to regulate AI, if you want to make it a tool that you use versus one you’re being replaced with — it’s all about collective action.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: A Decade of Bernie Sanders’s Transformation of America
articles.author: Meagan Day
articles.content: Over the past decade since his first presidential run, no one has done more to reshape the American left than Bernie Sanders. He is the most influential left-wing leader this country has seen since the 1960s, if not longer. While Sanders’s political career began decades earlier, his influence took on national dimensions ten years ago, when Sanders first campaigned for president against Hillary Clinton in the Democratic primary. He lost that campaign, but few losses have looked so much like a victory. Clinton has no political heirs openly claiming her legacy; indeed, today’s technocratic centrists squirm away from the association. Meanwhile, Sanders has dozens of self-professed acolytes at the federal level, hundreds or even thousands at the state and local levels, and an organization in the Democratic Socialists of America that, though he has never been a member, has grown from obscurity to 120,000 members since he first ran. Bernie Sanders’s first presidential campaign, then, is a significant event in twenty-first century American politics and the broader history of the American left, and its ten-year anniversary is a notable milestone. But Sanders himself hasn’t marked the occasion. Unlike most politicians, he demurs from telling his own story or touting his achievements. He’s also busy, playing a leading role in demanding artificial intelligence regulation and ending the war in Iran, with the next fight and the one after that. That laser focus on the present is why we love Bernie; it also means that commemorating and reflecting on the campaign that changed everything falls to us. At the top of any accounting of Sanders’s achievements since 2016 is the wave of young socialist elected officials he has inspired. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was a volunteer organizer for Sanders’s 2016 campaign, which she credits with motivating her to run for office. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has called Sanders “the single most influential political figure in my life” and has said it was “Bernie’s campaign for the presidency in 2016 that gave me the language of democratic socialism to describe my politics.” Sanders’s protégés in Congress now span two generations. There are the upperclassmen elected around 2018, including Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, and Rashida Tlaib. And pending November confirmation in their deep-blue districts, there’s now an incoming freshman class including Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, while several other Sanders acolytes, chief among them Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, are fighting through their general elections with a good shot at victory. Valdez best summarized this cohort’s indebtedness to Sanders when she said , “Three things made me a democratic socialist: sh–y jobs, the labor movement, and Bernie Sanders’s runs for president. His political revolution changed my life — and showed millions of Americans what’s possible when working people organize.” Sanders’s influence, however, is hardly restricted to office-seekers. His political orientation has reshaped the culture and strategic orientation of the American left as a whole. To appreciate how, recall what that culture looked like before he arrived. From the Battle of Seattle in 1999 through Occupy Wall Street in 2011, the American left was dominated by horizontalism, an anarchist-inflected politics that distrusted not only politicians and parties but mass politics itself. The Occupy-era left was suspicious of formal leadership, considered demands a concession to the system, and rarely organized itself beyond the affinity group or temporary action committees. The mobilizations of this period produced indelible images and genuinely radicalized participants, but they left behind no institutions capable of seriously contesting power. Meanwhile, those progressives who did continue to wage fights within the Democratic Party did so timidly and without ambition, failing to advance a robust legislative program and inspiring moral vision. Sanders offered an exit from both culs-de-sac. By running for president on a far-reaching program of reforms that were coherent and achievable but also highly audacious and transformative, he demonstrated that the Left could flourish by articulating clear demands and waging campaigns for Democratic Party nominations that were mostly independent of Democratic Party leadership. He showed that we could seek majorities and contest for power rather than just protest it — and that millions of ordinary people, mostly indifferent to the subcultural preoccupations of the already-existing activist left, would respond when we did. Bernie speaks at Transmitter Park in Brooklyn, New York, on April 8, 2016. (Timothy Krause / CC BY 2.0 ) If horizontalism was the radical left’s dominant tendency when Sanders arrived, identity politics was its successor in the decade that followed. The Right makes no distinction between the two emergent politics of the 2010s, Sanders-style democratic socialism and “wokeness.” In reality, however, Bernie Sanders has provided an alternate example for a left that otherwise finds it difficult to avoid the seductions of identity-based oppression rankings, elaborate deference pageantry, and shallow representational concerns. A universalist at heart, Sanders instead has modeled a politics genuinely progressive on civil rights and social equality that nonetheless declines the invitation to the culture wars, fixing its attention instead on what unites the broad working class rather than on the infinite ways it can be subdivided. That Sanders’s politics, forged in the crucible of the Free Speech and Civil Rights movements, remained wholly intact through the Left’s darkest decades is a testament to his idiosyncratic personality as much as his political convictions. Through sheer force of will, he has served as a bridge between the 1960s and our time. We’re lucky that a veteran of the nation’s last great left upsurge was still around to guide a new generation of democratic socialists — and that he had spent decades in office sorting what earlier generations got right from what they got wrong. There’s no one like Bernie Sanders. He remains singular today, even among the crop of leaders and activists who strive to emulate him. His obdurate universalism, unique and even comical ability to stay on message, and unyielding focus on issues of real importance to the long project of class struggle remain aspirational qualities. Society has not evolved past the need for Bernie Sanders. To mark the decade anniversary of Sanders’s first presidential campaign, we will be publishing a number of articles in the coming days by Jacobin contributors and contemporary socialist leaders reflecting on how the American left has changed since Bernie first ran. These articles will cover his impact on socialist organizations, his part in the still-unfinished effort to revitalize the labor movement, personal essays by socialist elected officials on his influence on them, and more. Though he’s far from finished remaking American politics, Sanders has already left a profound legacy that will not recede when he does eventually exit the public stage. Above all, he has broken the spell of demoralization that had settled over the American left, and over the working class itself. He has rekindled in millions of Americans the belief that things can change — that domination can be challenged, inequality overturned, injustice repaired, and power structures transformed in the interests of the many, not just the wealthy few. articles.title: Obama’s Monument to Empty Liberalism
articles.author: Natasha Lasky
articles.content: “When I first saw it, I was like, ‘It’s a block.’” Woodlawn resident Linda Spears had been watching the construction of the Obama Foundation’s sprawling campus from her condo overlooking Jackson Park in Chicago, but it wasn’t until opening weekend, when the barriers came down, that she finally went inside. Sitting on a bench near the Barack Obama Presidential Center’s playground, she recited the former president’s 2015 speech on the fiftieth anniversary of the Selma to Montgomery march from memory, as if echoing the words that appeared on the facade behind us. Spears explained that the museum tower at the Obama Presidential Center had actually been designed to resemble four hands reaching upward. She pressed her hands against those of a young woman beside her, as if playing patty-cake. “It’s like we’re all coming together,” she said. I saw this demonstration of the four hands many times during opening weekend, literally gesturing toward Obama’s vision of the center as “not just a monument to my presidency” but “a tribute to all the people and the forces and the community that helped to make this so special.” It’s an inspirational story every American liberal knows by heart: Obama arrived on the South Side of Chicago as a wayward twenty-three-year-old in a junky used car and left as the president of the United States. He envisioned the sprawling Obama Presidential Center campus as a thank-you gift to the city that created him, complete with a playground, a public library branch, gardens, and spaces for democratic education in a basement “forum.” On opening weekend, visitors lined up for paletas and Obama-themed merchandise at stands encouraging them to “bring change home.” They nodded along to Stevie Wonder’s live performance while inspecting hot peppers in the garden and wrote notes to Obama on index cards in the Forum basement and pinned them to the wall. Even on Sunday, when thunderstorms thinned out the crowds, a DJ shouted over the promenade, “We may be small in number, but we can make an impact.” Meanwhile, a cluster of visitors with umbrellas wobbled through the Electric Slide. Nowhere had I seen so many slogans: a T-shirt featuring Parks and Recreation ’s Ron Swanson with “I regret nothing” in Impact typeface, Future voter pins for the kids. Some seemed to be handmade — a group visiting from Mississippi had matching traffic-cone-orange shirts with Obama’s head superimposed on a photo of the Obama Center campus; the words “where we come to be inspired and change” appeared in white italics across the bottom. Another woman wore a white shirt with a wanted poster featuring Obama’s face. Above him read the headline “Have you seen this man? If so, can you please let him back into the White House?” Visitors would also see these kinds of handmade slogans and signs in the museum itself, relics from the civil rights movement and Harold Washington’s mayoral campaign as well as a display of 440 buttons from Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign — German-Americans for Obama, UAW for Obama–Biden, Vote Hope. The Obama museum’s celebration of the power of ordinary people may ring hollow, given the high-profile donors required to fund its $850 million budget. It’s difficult to sustain the cognitive dissonance of seeing an Occupy Wall Street display funded in part by Goldman Sachs and Bank of America, or stomach an exhibit about labor organizing after having wandered past a sign thanking Jeff Bezos. Even more ironic is the Obama Foundation’s apparent hostility to community organizers on the South Side. After the foundation announced in 2016 that the center would be built in Jackson Park, local faith organizations, tenant groups, and neighborhood associations formed a coalition to negotiate a community benefits agreement (CBA), a legally binding contract intended to protect Woodlawn residents from displacement. The foundation made a series of vague, voluntary commitments to community demands but chafed against the request to formalize them into a legally enforceable agreement. During a 2017 meeting, organizer and now alderwoman Jeanette Taylor asked Obama directly why he would not sign a CBA. “I was a community organizer,” Obama replied. “I know the neighborhood. I know that the minute you start saying, ‘Well, we’re thinking about signing something that will determine who’s getting jobs and contracts and this and that’ . . . next thing I know, I’ve got twenty organizations coming out of the woodwork.” It did not go over well. “He’s forgotten who he is,” Taylor later told a reporter. “He forgot the community got him where he is.” When Obama was elected to the Illinois State Senate in 1996, his wife, Michelle, said, “Barack is not a politician first and foremost. He’s a community activist exploring the viability of politics to make change.” In 2008, Sarah Palin mocked Obama’s lack of government experience from the Republican National Convention stage, sneering that “I guess a small-town mayor is sort of like a community organizer, except that you have actual responsibilities.” In his ascent to the Oval Office, Obama brought the question of what it means to be an organizer to the center of American politics. In the form of a near-billion-dollar museum, it seems that he has finally given his answer. On the third floor of the Obama museum, under a spotlight, is a magazine open to an article entitled “Why Organize? Problems and Promise in the Inner City.” In it, a twenty-seven-year-old Obama reflects on his time on the South Side. He begins the essay with an anecdote in which a public school administrative aide pulls him aside on a “bleak January morning” to ask why “a bright young man like [him] would go to college, get that degree and become a community organizer.” In the gentle, even-keeled mode that would eventually become his signature style, he argued that political and economic representation for black Chicagoans — in the form of elected officials like Harold Washington and “increased hiring of black contractors and corporate managers, or Buy Black campaigns” — had been largely “symbolic.” Only through organizing could the South Side harness its “internal productive capacities” toward systemic change. It is difficult to reconcile “Why Organize?” with the building in which it lives. The Obama Foundation celebrates the strategies that Obama had himself dismissed in 1988. Press releases proclaim the museum as a totem of Obama’s symbolic victory as the first black president and an engine of economic development on the South Side, “supporting thousands of jobs during and after construction.” The museum’s exhibits breeze past these contradictions. To wrap up Obama’s time as a community organizer, text strewn on the wall explains that “victories were rare,” and “Barack decided he could make a bigger difference in his community if he ran for elected office.” Filling in these gaps is a series of documents that line the walls. A couple years after “Why Organize?” was originally published in 1988, it appeared in an anthology, After Alinsky: Community Organizing in Illinois , reflecting on the legacy of Saul Alinsky , a towering figure in Chicago organizing. Alinsky tried to systematize the ad hoc techniques he encountered during a lifetime of organizing in Back of the Yards into a set of replicable methods, which he listed in his book Rules for Radicals (on sale at the Obama Center bookshop). Alinsky hoped to bring unions, churches, and other local groups together in a “People’s Organization” that could represent a neighborhood in perpetuity rather than wilting after the end of a particular campaign. At the age of twenty-three, after seeing a help wanted ad in The New York Times , Obama joined an attempt at one such organization, the Developing Communities Project (DCP), a coalition of Catholic parishes on Chicago’s far South Side. Obama’s bosses at the DCP, one of whom described himself as an Alinsky “disciple,” were trained in Alinsky’s methods. The museum displays a fax pinned to a wall, a lesson on Alinsky’s approach to coalition building, with Obama’s handwritten marginalia, notes like “self-interest” and “systemic,” in careful cursive. The museum includes little information about what Obama worked on at the DCP, save for a newspaper clipping from 1988. A grainy black-and-white photo shows a young Obama speaking to a couple of frowning white men, residents of Hegewisch, a southeastern Chicago neighborhood that borders Indiana. Hegewisch is enclosed by what activist Hazel M. Johnson called the “toxic doughnut,” a ring of landfills, highways, sewage treatment facilities, and chemical plants that pollute the surrounding neighborhoods. In his last months at the DCP, Obama was on a task force to prevent the development of new landfills through regulatory blockades. After he left for Harvard Law School later that year, the campaign won a moratorium on new waste sites. But fifty dumps and more than one hundred industrial plants remained, managed by both city agencies and private companies. The toxic doughnut exists to this day. In “Why Organize?,” Obama wrote that Chicago was haunted by the “skeletons” of these campaigns, dismayed to find that community organizing at the DCP felt more like cutting heads off a hydra than the David-and-Goliath fights he had romanticized before he took the job. Still, Obama had not abandoned Alinsky’s dream of the “People’s Organization” that could buoy movements across long-haul fights against overlapping public and private institutions. The future president wondered if he could “rework old models” of organizing like Alinsky’s “to fit new realities,” allowing community organizers, elected officials, and private companies to work hand in hand. The result of such a proposal was 2008’s Obama for America (OFA). OFA sought to imbue a presidential campaign with the energy of community organizing. Washington strategists set the agenda from the top down, but volunteers were encouraged to personalize it. Marshall Ganz, an activist and academic who helped shape the campaign’s organizing model, designed and led “Camp Obama,” volunteer training boot camps that were essentially storytelling workshops. Whether canvassing door-to-door or training new recruits, volunteers were instructed to move from “self” to “us” to “now”: beginning with a personal story, connecting it to the shared values of a community, and concluding with a call to action. Obama’s eventual victory was fueled by one of the largest volunteer organizations in American political history. The 440 campaign buttons lining a semicircle at the center of the museum’s third floor each represent five thousand campaign volunteers. Obama attempted to make OFA’s grassroots power permanent, transforming it first into Organizing for America (a project housed within the Democratic National Committee) and later into the independent nonprofit Organizing for Action. But the experiment proved difficult to sustain. Fundraising and staffing declined after 2012, and by 2018, Organizing for Action had merged into a redistricting committee before fizzling out altogether. Although it says little about Obama for America or Organizing for Action as institutions, the Obama Center Museum perfectly embodies Marshall Ganz’s three-act canvassing structure. The emotional climax of the campaign floor features a video of people around the world celebrating Obama’s election, complete with a box of tissues provided on a nearby chair. The galleries focused on the presidency years continue this move from “self” to “us” by showing the everyday people who benefited from Obama’s policies. There is the framed letter from Natoma Canfield, an Ohio cleaner who gained health insurance under the Affordable Care Act, and the wedding ring and marriage certificate of Jim Obergefell, the lead plaintiff in the Supreme Court case that legalized same-sex marriage nationwide. In the last few galleries, visitors are invited to design a campaign button of their own on an elaborate digital display before finally ascending to the “Sky Room” to look out at the city and reflect on their own capacity for action. But the Obama Presidential Center wants to do more than inspire visitors — it aims to be a civic institution capable of reshaping Woodlawn through a grab bag of community initiatives. It’s not as strange an ambition as it sounds. From its origins, the American presidential library has occupied an ambiguous space between public and private. When Franklin D. Roosevelt went looking for a way to institutionalize the preservation of presidential documents, he used the model of the National Gallery, which was then under construction, to structure his own archive: a private foundation would construct the building, while the federal government would maintain the records therein. He called this institution a library, a friendlier, folksier term than the imposing “archive,” with a clear connection to the public good. But as presidential libraries have ballooned in both size and construction costs in recent years — and become opportunities for elite fundraising — this system has been subject to increased scrutiny, as former presidents have saddled the federal government with the responsibility of maintaining increasingly palatial monuments to themselves. The Obama Foundation tried to skirt these controversies by cleaving the museum itself from the archive. Unlike traditional presidential libraries, the Obama Presidential Center contains no federally operated presidential records. Instead, the National Archives digitized and maintains Obama’s presidential records, while the Obama Foundation operates the museum independently. But the foundation has muddied the waters between private and public in other ways. In 2014, Mayor Rahm Emanuel , who once served as Obama’s chief of staff, allowed the Obama Foundation to appropriate acres of Jackson Park to build the presidential center. City officials put more than $123 million toward infrastructure improvements surrounding it. Resource appropriation on this scale was not uncommon for a presidential library under construction. The Commonwealth of Massachusetts purchased land from Boston’s transit authority for the JFK Library, while Lyndon B. Johnson’s library was constructed on public land donated by the University of Texas at Austin. Rather than going to war against the tangled web of public and private institutions he faced as a community organizer, Obama joined them. With a ninety-nine-year contract from the city and over $1 billion in assets, the Obama Presidential Center can make greater claims to permanence than OFA or the DCP ever could. Perhaps in that luxurious time frame, it can make good on its promise to transform Jackson Park into a “living, working center for citizenship.” Obama told The New Republic in 2007 that “people’s hopes and dreams and their ideals and their values were just as important in organizing as people’s self-interest.” His foundation describes the presidential center as “a place of dreaming,” and indeed, the Obama museum follows the tautological logic of a labyrinthine Escher staircase endlessly looping upward. Organizers of the past inspired Obama to become an organizer himself, and the people he met along the way inspired him to run for office, where he could inspire the public to elect him, who then inspired Obama to fight for them as president, who built a museum to inspire the public to take action yet again. This gives the museum’s anecdotes of public service a flat quality — all they are allowed to do is inspire. On touch screens throughout the building, you can see examples of ordinary people who participated in civic action, from abolishing a luxury tax on sanitary products in the UK to giving legal land titles to indigenous people in the Colombian Caribbean. The museum doesn’t say whether these efforts were insurgent or conciliatory, nor what kind of setbacks they faced or how communities responded, just as it does not dwell on the specifics of Obama’s campaigns as an organizer, the movements of the past that inspired him, or the troubles of his presidency. At the center’s opening ceremony, Obama remarked that his museum “won’t just be an exercise in nostalgia or looking backwards. We want to look forward.” But one cannot create a museum about something that has not happened yet, any more than one can create a top-down grassroots organization, a People’s Organization without the people.
